name: shadcn design
tagline: Paid Figma kit for shadcn/ui, plus coded Pro Blocks and a Figma-to-code plugin
description: A commercial design system that mirrors shadcn/ui in Figma across 8 named styles (Nova, Vega, Mira, Luma, Sera, Maia, Rhea, Lyra) in one file, with roughly 80 components and five bundled icon sets. On top of the kit it sells Pro Blocks — 202 verified landing-page blocks in 23 categories, plus 15 application and 11 e-commerce categories — available as Figma frames, and as React code in the Premium tier. It also ships a Figma plugin that exports variables and generates shadcn/ui + Next.js code, and Agent Skills files that teach Claude, Cursor, and Codex to convert its Figma frames into React. Aimed at product teams who design in Figma first and want the handoff to land on real shadcn/ui primitives.

Team Professional $359 / $999 / $1,599. Team Organization $459 / $1,199 / $1,799. Enterprise $999 / $1,999 / $3,499. 14-day refund at 90% of price.
agent_guidance: Reach for this only when the human side of the project already lives in Figma and you are being handed frames rather than a spec — its Agent Skills and plugin exist to make that handoff produce real shadcn/ui code instead of divs. If you just need React blocks, the free shadcn/ui blocks or an open registry get you there without a $559 licence, and nothing here installs from a public registry URL. Watch out that the 202 block figure is landing-page only and the React code is gated behind the Premium tier; Plus buyers get Figma frames with no code at all.
why_it_matters: The most complete paid Figma mirror of shadcn/ui, and one of the few design kits that has taken the Figma-to-agent handoff seriously with shipped skill files. The price ladder is steep and the code is locked to the top tier.

name: Skiper UI
tagline: 106 animated shadcn/ui components installed by registry, mostly behind a $129 licence
description: A shadcn-registry component library of showy, motion-heavy React pieces built with Tailwind and Motion — scroll effects, cursor trails, hover reveals, sign-in scenes, and lookalikes of things such as Dynamic Island and Vercel's tooltip. Every item is a single self-contained file with no extra packages, installed with the shadcn CLI from its own registry namespace. The sitemap enumerates 106 components, addressed as skiper1 through skiper107, and the registry JSON is publicly readable even for items the site paywalls. A free tier gives basic components; the rest need a one-time purchase.
pricing_detail: Free tier for basic components. Premium $129 one-time (all 106+ components, source, lifetime updates, early access). Exclusive $549 one-time (adds Figma file and full website templates, marked coming soon). No subscription.
agent_guidance: Use this when a brief asks for one specific viral interaction — a cursor trail, a snap-scroll hero, a Dynamic Island clone — and you want it as a single dependency-free file rather than wiring Motion by hand. The killer practical problem is that components are named skiper1..skiper107 with no semantic slugs, so you cannot guess an install target; read https://skiper-ui.com/sitemap.xml or the /r/{name}.json registry files to map a number to what it actually renders before installing. Treat these as decoration, not as a system: there is no documented accessibility work, and the paid tier's licence terms live only in the terms-of-service page.
why_it_matters: A real, working shadcn registry with genuinely uncommon motion pieces, held back by opaque numeric naming and a paywall over most of the catalogue.
notable_for: one file per component, no extra packages
evidence: https://skiper-ui.com/, https://skiper-ui.com/pricing, https://skiper-ui.com/sitemap.xml (220 URLs, 106 component slugs counted), https://skiper-ui.com/r/skiper40.json and /registry/skiper40.json (both return registry-item JSON). /docs and /components render as JS shells with no readable component names.

name: Codrops
tagline: Creative front-end tutorials, demos, and a 2,000-site showcase, running since 2009
description: The long-running publication for experimental front-end craft: step-by-step tutorials with working demos, case studies pulling apart how notable sites were built, and spotlights on studios, designers, and developers. Its Creative Hub collects Codrops originals and hand-picked demos, while Webzibition is a curated exhibition of over 2,000 standout websites. Posts land several times a week — entries dated 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, and 15 August 2026 were visible on the day of check. It is the reference point for WebGL, scroll, and motion techniques that later show up in component libraries.
agent_guidance: Search Codrops first when the ask is a technique rather than a component — a shader-backed hero, a scroll-driven page transition, an SVG distortion — because the tutorials ship the maths and a runnable demo, which a component registry never does. Pair it with Motion or GSAP for the animation layer; most demos are framework-free vanilla JS plus WebGL, so expect to port them into React yourself rather than installing anything. The demo licence is not stated in an obvious place, so check the footer License page before you lift code into a client project.
why_it_matters: Seventeen years of the deepest free writing on creative front-end work anywhere, and the place where the motion techniques the rest of the ecosystem copies get explained first.

name: Unicorn Studio
tagline: Browser tool that builds WebGL scenes and exports embeds for Framer, Webflow, or React
description: A no-code editor for real-time graphics: you stack shader effects, shapes, images, text, video, and 3D models on a layer-based canvas, then publish the scene as an embed. The docs list 75+ prebuilt effects, an AI-assisted creation mode, variables, presets, and an event system, with a production runtime of about 50 KB gzipped. Export buttons generate ready-made snippets for Framer, Webflow, Figma Sites, Wix, React/Next.js, and plain HTML; the runtime is unicornstudio.js, with unicornstudio-react on npm and data-us-* attributes for HTML containers. It needs WebGL2 and works best in Chrome.
pricing_detail: Reported, not verified first-hand: free plan gives all effects and up to 10 publishes, non-commercial only; Legend $14/month billed annually adds unlimited publishes, a commercial licence, 3D models, video hosting, versioning, and custom fonts. The pricing page did not render for a direct fetch.
agent_guidance: Reach for this when a design calls for a bespoke animated shader background and hand-writing GLSL or wiring three.js would eat the budget — the output is a project ID plus a ~50 KB runtime, not source you own. In React, install unicornstudio-react and pass the project ID; in plain HTML use the data-us-project attribute and call UnicornStudio.init() to get the scene handles for setting variables at runtime. Two traps: the free tier forbids commercial use, so any client work needs the paid plan, and every scene is a hosted third-party dependency with a hard WebGL2 requirement — always ship a static fallback.
why_it_matters: It puts production WebGL in reach of designers who will never write a shader, and it is the tool behind a large share of the glossy Framer and Webflow sites of the last two years.
notable_for: one-click exports for Framer, Webflow, Figma Sites, React
evidence: https://www.unicorn.studio/docs/ and https://www.unicorn.studio/docs/embed/ read cleanly. https://www.unicorn.studio/, /home/, and /pricing return 200 but render as empty JS shells with only the title; pricing figures come from a web search of secondary sources and are flagged as unverified.

name: AI Tools Registry
tagline: shadcn-CLI registry of 15 Vercel AI SDK tools with matching React renderers
description: A small open registry that ships AI SDK v5 tool definitions — image generation, web search, weather, news, USGS earthquake stats, QR codes — as plain files you add with the shadcn CLI, each with an optional React renderer such as WeatherCard or NewsList. Provider variants are separate registry items, so you install @ai-tools/websearch-exa or @ai-tools/image-fal rather than configuring one abstraction. Built with Next.js, TypeScript, shadcn/ui, and Zod; several tools need their own API key. A @ai-tools/tool-pack item installs the whole set at once.
agent_guidance: Use this to skip writing boilerplate AI SDK tool definitions — the Zod schemas, the fetch, and a card renderer arrive together, which is faster than hand-rolling a weather or web-search tool for a chat demo. Prefer it over writing your own only for the throwaway or prototype case: the repo has no LICENSE file and its last push was December 2025, so for anything shipped, read the installed file, pin the AI SDK version, and expect to maintain it yourself. Provider variants are separate items, so pick @ai-tools/websearch-exa or -brave deliberately and check which API keys each one wants before installing the tool-pack.
why_it_matters: A neat demonstration that the shadcn registry format works for server-side agent tools, not just UI, but it is one maintainer's side project with no licence and eight months of quiet.
notable_for: 15 registry items covering image, search, weather, news, QR

name: Pattern Craft
tagline: 257 copy-paste CSS background patterns and gradients, MIT licensed
description: A free gallery of background treatments you copy as CSS or Tailwind-ready snippets, filed under Gradients, Geometric, Decorative, and Effects, with a favourites filter. Every pattern has a live preview and one-click copy, uses no external dependencies, and is written for JSX and React as well as plain HTML. The site counts 257 patterns; the MIT-licensed repo has about 3.1k stars and was pushed in July 2026, and it is part of the Vercel OSS Program.
agent_guidance: Reach for this the moment a hero or section looks flat and you need a background in one line — it beats generating gradient CSS yourself because each snippet is already tuned and dependency-free. Prefer it over Unicorn Studio or a canvas library whenever the effect can be static, since these are pure CSS with no runtime, no WebGL requirement, and no third-party host. Two cautions: most patterns are a single absolutely positioned div you must place behind content with the right z-index, and several rely on radial-gradient stacks that read very differently on a dark background, so check both themes.
why_it_matters: The quickest honest fix for the blank-background problem, MIT licensed and large enough that you rarely need a second source.
